task_description: Help me draft an email to our engineering team about pushing the product launch date by two weeks due to a critical bug we found in testing.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that land with clarity and respect — readers should know exactly what happened, why it matters to them, and what to do next. Values emotional intelligence in sequencing and refuses to waste a reader's time.

rubric.name: Emotional Arc Sequencing
rubric.description: Information follows a strict order: acknowledge the situation or effort first (1 sentence max), then deliver the core message, then explain why it matters from the reader's perspective, then state the next step. Violating this order — even if all elements are present — makes the email feel wrong.

dimensions.label: Opens with a brief acknowledgment of the reader's context or effort before delivering the main point
Explains why the news matters AFTER stating it, not before
Stakes are framed from the reader's perspective ('your team planned around this') not the sender's ('we want quality')
The call to action is the last substantive element — nothing trails after it

rubric.name: Single-Owner Action Items
rubric.description: When action is needed, names ONE clear owner with a deadline rather than diffuse group asks. 'Everyone please review' is treated as a non-action. But avoids over-specifying org structure details the email shouldn't contain.

dimensions.label: Each action item has a single named person responsible, not a group
Action items include a specific deadline or timeframe
Avoids diffuse asks like 'everyone please' or 'team, let's all'
Does not assume or dictate internal team structure, delegation, or process the sender wouldn't know

rubric.name: No Trailing Sentiment
rubric.description: Closing lines are forward-looking and action-oriented. No 'thanks for your patience,' motivational platitudes, or filler sentiment after the CTA. The email ends when the action is stated.

dimensions.label: The closing line references a future action or outcome, not past effort or gratitude
Does not end with generic encouragement ('excited about this!', 'great work team!')
Nothing substantive appears after the call to action — no trailing paragraphs or softening

rubric.name: Compression Without Ambiguity
rubric.description: Every sentence earns its place, but brevity never creates confusion. Prefers cutting entire points over compressing them into dense, hard-to-parse sentences.

dimensions.label: No sentence restates information already conveyed in another sentence
Removes low-priority points entirely rather than squeezing them into subordinate clauses
Each sentence carries one main idea — no run-ons or stacked clauses

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Alex treats email as a precision tool — every structural choice signals respect for the reader's time and emotional state. Will reject drafts that have all the right content in the wrong order. Non-negotiable: the reader's perspective drives the 'why', never the sender's.

rounds.draft:
**Subject: Product Launch Rescheduled — New Date: [Date]**

Hi team,

You've put serious work into getting ready for the [original date] launch, and I want to make sure you have the full picture before plans solidify further.

We're moving the launch back two weeks to [new date]. During final testing, we identified a critical bug that would have affected [briefly describe impact, e.g., "core checkout functionality for users"]. Shipping with it wasn't an option.

This affects your sprint planning, any external commitments you've made around the original date, and coordination with other teams — so the sooner you can adjust, the better.

**[Name]**, please update the launch calendar and notify any dependent teams by [specific date/time].

criteria.justification: The email opens with a one-sentence acknowledgment of the reader's effort ('You've put serious work into getting ready'), then delivers the core message (launch moved to new date), then explains why it matters from the reader's perspective (sprint planning, external commitments, coordination), and ends with the CTA as the final element. All four steps are in correct order. The only minor issue is the phrase 'I want to make sure you have the full picture before plans solidify further' in the opening sentence slightly blurs the acknowledgment with a sender-framing rationale, but it doesn't violate the arc meaningfully.

The action item names a single person ('[Name]'), specifies exactly what they should do (update the launch calendar and notify dependent teams), and includes a specific deadline ('[specific date/time]'). There are no group asks, and the email does not over-specify internal delegation or org structure beyond what the sender would reasonably know.

The email ends precisely at the call to action — no gratitude, no platitudes, no softening language after the CTA. The closing is clean and forward-looking, referencing a concrete future action (updating the calendar and notifying teams by a deadline).

The draft is tight and each sentence carries a distinct idea. The stakes paragraph ('This affects your sprint planning...') efficiently lists impacts without redundancy. Otherwise, no run-ons or stacked clauses are present.
